parts.text: There is growing evidence that children today have fewer opportunities for independent, adventurous

play and fewer chances to make decisions and shape their own experiences than previous generations.

Just 43% of children and young people aged from eight to 15 in England report spending time outdoors every day or most days. Research suggests that outdoor play has

by 50% within a generation.

Despite this decline, outdoor play is still often viewed as an opportunity for children to learn to manage risk and develop both their confidence and independence.

My research

how children make decisions when playing outside. The findings suggested that when young children hold back and resist risky play outdoors, it is rarely because they lack confidence or even access. Instead, they are responding to the subtle messages adults

about risk, mess and safety.

I carried out the research in a school, in collaboration with a nursery teacher. Our participants were children aged three to five who were enrolled in nursery and reception, meaning the school’s outdoor environment was

to them.

We combined observations of children’s play with small focus groups in which children took photographs to show what they liked and disliked about their outdoor environment. From these early conversations with the children,

patterns emerged. These children tended to avoid areas they associated with discomfort or danger, such as mud, water and climbing equipment, even though these spaces were familiar to them and adults were not

their access.

Children expressed things such as “I might fall”, “I don’t want to get wet”, and “My teacher doesn’t let me”. These were not spontaneous fears; they were reflections of the messages the children had

heard from adults.

During our observations, we heard staff within the setting sometimes offering cautions such as “be careful”, “don’t climb too high”, and “watch out” during the children’s free play within the outdoors environment.

During our

conversations with the children, they also described similar warnings from parents and carers. One child explained, “My mum doesn’t let me climb because I bumped my nose once”. These repeated messages had a lasting impact on how the children
risk. Over time, they absorbed these warnings and began to guide their own behaviour. Their hesitancy was learned, not innate.
